subtopic_detail: Late preterm hypoglycaemia intervention threshold and glucose gel first-line
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar in the postnatal ward reviewing a 36 plus 4 week baby girl born by uncomplicated vaginal delivery 3 hours ago. Birthweight is 2450 g. Her mother has type 2 diabetes managed on metformin during pregnancy. The baby is skin-to-skin, has latched but only briefly, and looks pink and settled. The midwife has performed the routine pre-feed heel-prick glucose per the trust pathway.

On examination she is alert, well perfused, and euvolaemic. There is no jitteriness, tone is normal, and the cry is strong. Vital signs: pulse 148/min, respiratory rate 44/min, SpO2 98 percent in room air, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius. The pre-feed heel-prick blood glucose is 2.2 mmol/L (above 2.6). Umbilical cord pH was 7.32 with base excess minus 2.

data_table.Baby: 36+4 weeks; 2450 g; 3 hours old; skin-to-skin; alert and pink; no jitteriness
data_table.Risk factor: Mother with type 2 diabetes on metformin during pregnancy

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Give a single formula top-up feed of 15 mL/kg and defer repeat glucose testing until the next routine 3 hour check
options.rationale: Formula alone without dextrose gel takes longer to correct the glucose and dextrose gel with breastfeeding is proven to reduce NICU admission; deferring repeat testing to the next 3 hour check misses a rebound below 2.6 (Source: RANZCOG and ADIPS Consensus on Neonatal Hypoglycaemia).
source_refs: RANZCOG and ADIPS Consensus on Neonatal Hypoglycaemia

options.text: Give buccal 40 percent dextrose gel 200 mg/kg, feed at the breast, and repeat the blood glucose in 30 minutes
options.rationale: The ANZ Neonatal Network hypoglycaemia pathway makes 40 percent dextrose gel 200 mg/kg (0.5 mL/kg) plus a feed the first-line response to asymptomatic hypoglycaemia (BSL under 2.6) in an at-risk late-preterm baby, with repeat glucose in 30 minutes to guide escalation (Source: RANZCOG and ADIPS Consensus on Neonatal Hypoglycaemia).
source_refs: RANZCOG and ADIPS Consensus on Neonatal Hypoglycaemia

options.text: Transfer to the neonatal unit for an intravenous 10 percent glucose infusion at 4 mg/kg/min
options.rationale: Intravenous glucose is reserved for symptomatic hypoglycaemia, glucose under 1.5 mmol/L, or failure of dextrose gel plus feed to correct the BSL; separating this baby from the mother now is disproportionate to a single asymptomatic pre-feed reading of 2.2 mmol/L (Source: RANZCOG and ADIPS Consensus on Neonatal Hypoglycaemia).
source_refs: RANZCOG and ADIPS Consensus on Neonatal Hypoglycaemia

options.text: Reassure the mother, encourage continued skin-to-skin, and repeat the glucose after the next feed in 3 hours
options.rationale: A late-preterm infant of a diabetic mother with a documented BSL of 2.2 mmol/L requires active correction, not observation for 3 hours which risks progression to symptomatic hypoglycaemia and neurodevelopmental harm (Source: RANZCOG and ADIPS Consensus on Neonatal Hypoglycaemia).
source_refs: RANZCOG and ADIPS Consensus on Neonatal Hypoglycaemia

options.text: Administer intramuscular glucagon 0.2 mg/kg and continue routine breastfeeding on the postnatal ward
options.rationale: Intramuscular glucagon is reserved for refractory or symptomatic hypoglycaemia where intravenous access is delayed; it is not the initial response to an asymptomatic BSL of 2.2 mmol/L when dextrose gel and a feed will correct most episodes (Source: RANZCOG and ADIPS Consensus on Neonatal Hypoglycaemia).
source_refs: RANZCOG and ADIPS Consensus on Neonatal Hypoglycaemia

explanation.summary: The AU pathway for asymptomatic at-risk neonatal hypoglycaemia (late preterm, infant of diabetic mother, macrosomia, or small-for-gestational-age) starts with 40 percent dextrose gel 200 mg/kg buccally with a supported breastfeed, then repeats the glucose in 30 minutes. This protocol reduces NICU admission and preserves breastfeeding and skin-to-skin. Intravenous glucose is reserved for symptomatic infants, a BSL under 1.5 mmol/L, or a failed gel-plus-feed trial. Glucagon is a niche rescue for refractory hypoglycaemia awaiting intravenous access.
key_points: Asymptomatic at-risk baby with BSL under 2.6 mmol/L: dextrose gel 200 mg/kg plus feed first
Repeat glucose 30 minutes after gel to guide escalation
Intravenous 10 percent dextrose only for symptomatic, BSL under 1.5, or gel-and-feed failure
explanation.pearls: Dextrose gel has been shown to reduce NICU admission when used first-line in asymptomatic neonatal hypoglycaemia; it does not replace a feed but keeps mother and baby together.

sources.label: RANZCOG and ADIPS Consensus on Neonatal Hypoglycaemia
Australian and New Zealand Neonatal Network Clinical Practice Guidelines

subtopic_detail: Duct-dependent congenital heart disease and prostaglandin E1
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called to the neonatal unit for a 3 day old term boy referred by a GP after his mother noticed him going 'grey' during feeds. He was discharged home well on day 1 after an unremarkable postnatal course. There is no family history of congenital heart disease and the antenatal 20 week morphology ultrasound was reported as normal.

On examination he is pale and mildly cool with reduced femoral pulses compared to brachials. There is a soft grade 2 systolic murmur at the left sternal border. Vital signs: pre-ductal SpO2 96 percent in the right hand, post-ductal SpO2 82 percent in the right foot, pulse 168/min, blood pressure 62/38 mmHg right arm and 44/26 mmHg right leg, respiratory rate 58/min, temperature 36.4 degrees Celsius. Arterial blood gas shows pH 7.28, lactate 6.2 mmol/L (0.5 to 2.2), and glucose 3.9 mmol/L.

data_table.Age and background: 3 day old term male; discharged well; antenatal morphology normal
data_table.Saturation split: Pre-ductal 96 percent right hand; post-ductal 82 percent right foot
data_table.Blood pressure split: 62/38 mmHg right arm; 44/26 mmHg right leg
data_table.Perfusion: Pale, mildly cool, reduced femoral pulses
data_table.Bloods: pH 7.28; lactate 6.2 mmol/L (0.5 to 2.2); glucose 3.9 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial pharmacological step?

options.text: Commence intravenous prostaglandin E1 at 10 to 20 ng/kg/min while arranging urgent cardiology transfer
options.rationale: The saturation and blood pressure splits with metabolic acidosis point to a duct-dependent systemic circulation such as coarctation or interrupted arch; prostaglandin E1 maintains ductal patency and buys time for cardiac assessment and surgical planning (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Newborn).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Newborn

options.text: Start intravenous adrenaline infusion at 0.1 microgram/kg/min for presumed cardiogenic shock now
options.rationale: Inotropic support without opening the duct addresses the wrong physiology; adrenaline may increase myocardial oxygen demand and worsen ischaemia in a duct-dependent lesion before prostaglandin restores systemic flow (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Newborn).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Newborn

options.text: Give intravenous frusemide 1 mg/kg and start oral captopril for presumed coarctation of the aorta
options.rationale: Frusemide and afterload reduction do not maintain ductal patency and worsen perfusion in a duct-dependent circulation before echocardiography and surgery; prostaglandin is the immediate stabilising drug (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Newborn).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Newborn

options.text: Give 20 mL/kg saline bolus with intravenous ceftriaxone and admit for suspected late-onset sepsis
options.rationale: Volume loading a duct-dependent systemic circulation can precipitate pulmonary oedema and cardiovascular collapse and antibiotics without prostaglandin do not address the anatomical driver of the shock (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Newborn).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Newborn

options.text: Provide 100 percent oxygen via facemask and continue observation on the postnatal ward for now
options.rationale: High-flow oxygen can accelerate ductus arteriosus closure, worsening a duct-dependent lesion; the pre-post ductal split needs prostaglandin, not more oxygen, and this baby requires transfer not ward observation (Source: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Newborn).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Newborn

explanation.summary: A well-appearing term newborn presenting on day 2 to 3 with poor feeding, pre-post ductal saturation split, reduced femoral pulses, and metabolic acidosis has a duct-dependent systemic circulation until proven otherwise. The single stabilising drug is prostaglandin E1 at 10 to 20 nanograms/kg/min, which maintains patency of the ductus arteriosus and restores systemic flow. Antibiotics may run in parallel if sepsis is a competing possibility but should not delay prostaglandin. Volume loading and high-flow oxygen are actively harmful in this setting.
key_points: Pre-post ductal saturation split plus reduced femoral pulses suggests duct-dependent systemic circulation
Prostaglandin E1 10 to 20 ng/kg/min stabilises before echocardiography and transfer
Avoid high-flow oxygen and large volume loading before ductal patency is secured
explanation.pearls: Duct closes physiologically around day 2 to 5, which is when duct-dependent lesions unmask; a pre-post ductal saturation difference of at least 3 percent flags urgent cardiology assessment.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Congenital Heart Disease in the Newborn

subtopic_detail: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia salt-losing crisis in a neonate
stem:
You are the paediatric registrar called to review a 12 day old baby boy in a regional emergency department. He has been vomiting for 3 days and has lost 12 percent of birthweight. He was born at term with an unremarkable delivery and was discharged home well on day 2 with normal newborn screening bloods pending. There is no diarrhoea and no fever, and his mother has been unwell with a viral illness for 5 days.

On examination he is lethargic with dry mucous membranes and a sunken fontanelle. External genitalia are anatomically male with mildly hyperpigmented scrotal skin. Vital signs: pulse 178/min, blood pressure 58/32 mmHg, respiratory rate 52/min, SpO2 98 percent in room air, temperature 36.6 degrees Celsius. Capillary refill is 4 seconds. Investigations: sodium 122 mmol/L (135 to 145), potassium 6.8 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.0), glucose 2.4 mmol/L, bicarbonate 14 mmol/L (22 to 32), urea 12.8 mmol/L (2.5 to 7.5).

data_table.Age and history: 12 day old term male; vomiting 3 days; 12 percent weight loss; mother had a viral illness
data_table.Vitals: HR 178; BP 58/32; RR 52; SpO2 98 percent; T 36.6
data_table.Examination: Lethargic; dry mucous membranes; sunken fontanelle; hyperpigmented scrotal skin
data_table.Bloods: Na 122 mmol/L; K 6.8 mmol/L; glucose 2.4 mmol/L; HCO3 14 mmol/L; urea 12.8 mmol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Give 20 mL/kg saline bolus and start intravenous ceftriaxone 50 mg/kg for suspected neonatal sepsis
options.rationale: Missing steroid replacement in a salt-losing crisis is a fatal omission even with fluid and antibiotics; sepsis may coexist but hydrocortisone must not wait, and 20 mL/kg initial bolus is larger than the RCH neonatal pathway recommends in the absence of overt shock signs (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal Crisis).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Adrenal Crisis

options.text: Commence oral fludrocortisone 100 microgram daily and rehydrate slowly with oral electrolyte solution
options.rationale: Oral fludrocortisone alone acts too slowly to reverse a salt-losing crisis and this shocked vomiting neonate cannot rely on oral rehydration; intravenous fluid and parenteral hydrocortisone are needed first (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal Crisis).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Adrenal Crisis

options.text: Give 10 mL/kg saline bolus, correct glucose with 10 percent dextrose, and start intravenous hydrocortisone 25 mg stat
options.rationale: This picture of hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, and shock in a term male neonate on day 12 fits a salt-losing crisis in classical congenital adrenal hyperplasia; RCH pathway is fluid and glucose resuscitation with parenteral hydrocortisone as a stat 25 mg dose in neonates, and blood for 17-hydroxyprogesterone before ongoing hydrocortisone is essential to lock in the diagnosis (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal Crisis).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Adrenal Crisis

options.text: Administer intravenous calcium gluconate and salbutamol nebuliser for the hyperkalaemia as first step
options.rationale: Hyperkalaemia treatment without addressing the underlying adrenal insufficiency does not correct the driving pathology; hydrocortisone plus saline and dextrose start the definitive treatment and typically bring potassium down without calcium or nebulised beta-agonist (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal Crisis).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Adrenal Crisis

options.text: Give 3 percent hypertonic saline 3 mL/kg to correct sodium at 8 mmol/L per hour and observe closely
options.rationale: Rapid correction of hyponatraemia in a hypovolaemic child risks central pontine myelinolysis; the driver is aldosterone deficiency and sodium corrects gradually once fluid and hydrocortisone are given (Source: RCH CPG: Adrenal Crisis).
source_refs: RCH CPG: Adrenal Crisis

explanation.summary: A 2 week old boy with hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia, and shock has a salt-losing crisis of 21-hydroxylase deficiency until proven otherwise, because male infants have no ambiguous genitalia to flag the diagnosis earlier. The immediate treatment is fluid and glucose correction with parenteral hydrocortisone (25 mg stat in neonates), then continued hydrocortisone at stress dose. Blood for 17-hydroxyprogesterone must be drawn before the second hydrocortisone dose so newborn-screen confirmation is possible. Hyperkalaemia rarely needs additional treatment once hydrocortisone and volume are given.
key_points: Hyponatraemia plus hyperkalaemia plus hypoglycaemia plus shock in a 2 week old male = CAH salt-losing crisis
Hydrocortisone 25 mg stat and saline resuscitation are the immediate steps
explanation.pearls: Male CAH typically presents around day 7 to 14 as a salt-losing crisis because there is no genital ambiguity to prompt earlier diagnosis; newborn screening turnaround in Australia is usually about 1 week.

sources.label: APEG Position Statement on Congenital Adrenal Hyperplasia

subtopic_detail: Second-line uterotonic after failed oxytocin and ergometrine
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a level 3 maternity unit called to a 32 year old primipara 20 minutes after a spontaneous vaginal birth at 39 weeks. Estimated blood loss is 1400 mL and she is still bleeding briskly per vaginum with a soft boggy uterus. Baseline blood pressure at booking was 118/74 mmHg and antenatal course was unremarkable. She has no known allergies and no personal or family history of asthma.

She has received oxytocin 10 units intramuscular at the birth of the anterior shoulder, an oxytocin infusion 40 units in 1 L Hartmann's solution over 4 hours, and ergometrine 250 microgram intramuscular 5 minutes ago. The bladder is empty. The perineum shows a small superficial midline tear that is not bleeding. Vital signs: pulse 118/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 22/min, SpO2 99 percent, temperature 36.9 degrees Celsius.

data_table.Vitals: HR 118; BP 96/58; RR 22; SpO2 99 percent; T 36.9
data_table.Uterotonics given: Oxytocin 10 units IM at birth; oxytocin 40 units in 1 L Hartmann's over 4 hours; ergometrine 250 microgram IM 5 minutes ago
data_table.Genital tract: Small superficial midline tear, not bleeding

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next uterotonic to administer?

options.text: Repeat ergometrine 250 microgram intramuscular immediately as a doubled second dose
options.rationale: Ergometrine is capped at a maximum of 500 microgram in 24 hours and its second dose is not the recommended next escalation when uterine tone remains poor; RANZCOG moves to a prostaglandin (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 43a Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage).
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 43a Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage

options.text: Carboprost 250 microgram intramuscular, may repeat every 15 minutes up to a total of 2 mg
options.rationale: RANZCOG PPH pathway steps from oxytocin to ergometrine to carboprost 250 microgram intramuscular for continuing atonic bleeding; carboprost is safe here because there is no history of asthma (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 43a Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage).
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 43a Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage

options.text: Misoprostol 800 microgram sublingual as the next uterotonic in place of carboprost
options.rationale: Misoprostol is the RANZCOG fallback when parenteral uterotonics are unavailable or contraindicated; carboprost is preferred as second-line when the woman has no asthma contraindication because it acts faster and more reliably than misoprostol (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 43a Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage).
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 43a Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage

options.text: Initiate a magnesium sulfate loading dose of 4 g intravenous over 20 minutes to relax the uterine vasculature
options.rationale: Magnesium sulfate is not a PPH uterotonic and would relax the uterus and worsen atony; its role is eclampsia neuroprophylaxis, not haemorrhage (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 43a Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage).
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 43a Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage

options.text: Recombinant activated factor VII 90 microgram/kg intravenous before further uterotonic escalation
options.rationale: Recombinant factor VIIa is a last-resort haemostatic adjunct after failure of uterotonics, mechanical measures, and surgical control, and only when specific coagulation targets have been met; using it now bypasses the standard escalation ladder (Source: RANZCOG C-Obs 43a Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage).
source_refs: RANZCOG C-Obs 43a Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage

explanation.summary: Atonic PPH follows a sequential uterotonic ladder: oxytocin bolus then infusion, ergometrine (if no hypertension), and carboprost 250 microgram intramuscular every 15 minutes up to 2 mg as third-line where asthma is not a contraindication. Tranexamic acid 1 g intravenous should be given within 3 hours of birth alongside these steps. Misoprostol 800 microgram is the sublingual fallback where parenteral options are unavailable or contraindicated. Recombinant factor VIIa and intrauterine balloon are reserved for continuing haemorrhage after uterotonic failure with correction of coagulopathy.
key_points: Third-line uterotonic in PPH: carboprost 250 microgram IM every 15 minutes to 2 mg total
Ergometrine capped at 500 microgram in 24 hours and avoided in hypertension
Give tranexamic acid 1 g intravenous within 3 hours of birth alongside uterotonic escalation
explanation.pearls: Carboprost is a bronchoconstrictor; ask about asthma before drawing it up because that single question changes the answer to sublingual misoprostol.

sources.label: RANZCOG C-Obs 43a Management of Postpartum Haemorrhage

subtopic_detail: First-line pharmacotherapy when diet and metformin fail
stem:
You are the obstetric registrar in a diabetes-in-pregnancy clinic seeing a 33 year old woman at 30 weeks gestation with dietary-diagnosed gestational diabetes at 26 weeks (fasting glucose 5.4 mmol/L, 2 hour 8.9 mmol/L on 75 g OGTT). She has followed the dietitian's plan for 4 weeks and metformin was uptitrated to 2 g daily 2 weeks ago. She has had no hypoglycaemia symptoms and is otherwise well; her weight gain has been within target and foetal growth is on the 45th centile.

Her 2 week home glucose diary shows fasting values consistently between 5.4 and 5.9 mmol/L (target under 5.1) with post-prandial readings on target. Vital signs and urinalysis are unremarkable and blood pressure today is 118/72 mmHg.

data_table.Gestation: 30 weeks with GDM diagnosed at 26 weeks
data_table.Current management: Dietary intervention for 4 weeks; metformin 2 g daily for 2 weeks
data_table.Home glucose diary: Fasting 5.4 to 5.9 mmol/L (target <5.1); postprandial on target

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in glycaemic management?

options.text: Continue current therapy and repeat the 75 g oral glucose tolerance test in 4 weeks
options.rationale: Repeat OGTT does not add information once GDM is diagnosed and treated; the fasting values already exceed target and demand pharmacological escalation rather than diagnostic reassessment (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for the Testing and Diagnosis of Hyperglycaemia in Pregnancy in Australia and New Zealand).
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for the Testing and Diagnosis of Hyperglycaemia in Pregnancy in Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Add rapid-acting insulin lispro before each main meal targeted at post-prandial glucose control
options.rationale: Post-prandial values are within target so mealtime rapid-acting insulin does not address the fasting problem and adds unnecessary hypoglycaemia risk; basal insulin is the intervention that fits the specific pattern (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for the Testing and Diagnosis of Hyperglycaemia in Pregnancy in Australia and New Zealand).
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for the Testing and Diagnosis of Hyperglycaemia in Pregnancy in Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Add bedtime intermediate-acting isophane insulin titrated to target fasting glucose under 5.1 mmol/L
options.rationale: ADIPS guidance recommends adding basal insulin when fasting glucose remains above target despite metformin and diet in GDM, with bedtime isophane titrated to the fasting target; long-acting analogue insulin is a reasonable alternative but isophane remains the ADIPS default (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for the Testing and Diagnosis of Hyperglycaemia in Pregnancy in Australia and New Zealand).
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for the Testing and Diagnosis of Hyperglycaemia in Pregnancy in Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Increase the metformin dose to 3 g daily divided across three meals to overcome the residual fasting elevation
options.rationale: Maximum recommended metformin in pregnancy is 2 g daily; further increase does not improve glycaemic outcomes and increases gastrointestinal intolerance without addressing the fasting profile that specifically responds to basal insulin (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for the Testing and Diagnosis of Hyperglycaemia in Pregnancy in Australia and New Zealand).
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for the Testing and Diagnosis of Hyperglycaemia in Pregnancy in Australia and New Zealand

options.text: Stop metformin and commence glibenclamide 2.5 mg twice daily as the primary sulphonylurea for GDM
options.rationale: Glibenclamide is not recommended in Australian GDM practice because it crosses the placenta and is associated with neonatal hypoglycaemia and macrosomia compared to insulin (Source: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for the Testing and Diagnosis of Hyperglycaemia in Pregnancy in Australia and New Zealand).
source_refs: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for the Testing and Diagnosis of Hyperglycaemia in Pregnancy in Australia and New Zealand

explanation.summary: In gestational diabetes, glycaemic targets are fasting under 5.1 mmol/L and 2 hour post-prandial under 6.7 mmol/L. When lifestyle plus metformin at maximum dose (2 g/day) do not achieve the fasting target, ADIPS recommends adding a basal insulin at bedtime, titrated to the fasting glucose. Rapid-acting mealtime insulin is added later if post-prandial values are also out of range. Sulphonylureas such as glibenclamide are avoided because of placental transfer and neonatal hypoglycaemia. Foetal ultrasound should be repeated at 34 to 36 weeks to guide timing of birth.
key_points: GDM fasting target under 5.1 mmol/L; add basal insulin when metformin fails to reach it
Rapid-acting insulin added mealtime only if post-prandial values exceed 6.7 mmol/L
Sulphonylureas avoided in AU because of placental transfer and neonatal hypoglycaemia
explanation.pearls: The pattern of glucose failure decides the insulin: fasting hyperglycaemia needs basal, post-prandial needs mealtime; treating the wrong pattern wastes hypoglycaemia budget.

sources.label: ADIPS Consensus Guidelines for the Testing and Diagnosis of Hyperglycaemia in Pregnancy in Australia and New Zealand
RANZCOG C-Obs 7 Diagnosis of Gestational Diabetes Mellitus
